Manual checking limits autonomy but is appropriate before testing whether the activity deserves automation.

evidence.scope: Official EU aggregate context; not evidence of Riga buyers or willingness to pay.
evidence.quote: In 2025, household final consumption expenditure, corrected for inflation, grew by 1.6% in the EU compared with 2024.

uncertainty: Riga parents in one parent-selected child age band repeatedly want short shared observation activities and find existing options less convenient.
Parents might eventually pay for consistently suitable, ready-to-use cards; museums might fund educational distribution. No supplied receipt establishes either willingness or budget.

Proposed test, not yet run: with permission, invite ten families through parent groups to try two manually reviewed challenges in one week at €0. Pass only if at least four voluntarily complete the second challenge without reminders, confirmed through minimal parent-only reporting.
Ask participating parents what activity the cards replaced and why they chose them; compare with their existing activities and awareness of the cited museum programme.
No parent interviews, participation, repeat use or payment evidence exists.
dissent: The museum announcement may indicate an existing alternative rather than an unmet need; it does not establish a family-specific problem.
A free first completion could reflect novelty or politeness. Even voluntary second use would support only short-term repeat value, not paid demand.
A payer is not necessary for this bounded free pilot, but sustained free provision would still require a credible funding and workload model.
